title: Wind and weather in the Kali Gandaki valley
meta_description: Why the Kali Gandaki wind blows every afternoon, why Jomsom flights leave at dawn, and Mustang's weather month by month, from rain shadow to winter cold.
summary: Mustang lies in the rain shadow of the Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges, so it is dry when the rest of Nepal is wet. Its defining weather is the wind: every day from late morning a strong wind blows up the Kali Gandaki gorge until evening, which is why flights to Jomsom leave at dawn and walkers start early.

sections.heading: A valley that cuts through the Himalaya
paras: The Kali Gandaki is older than the mountains around it. As the Himalaya rose, the river kept cutting down, and today it flows south from the Tibetan side of the range straight between two peaks over 8,000 m, Dhaulagiri to the west and Annapurna I to the east. Measured from those summits to the river, the gorge is more than 5,000 m deep, and it is often called one of the deepest in the world.

That geography shapes everything about the weather. South of the main range, around Tatopani and Ghasa, monsoon clouds pile up against the mountains and drop heavy rain. North of it, around Jomsom, Kagbeni and Lo Manthang, the same clouds have already lost most of their moisture. In a few hours' drive you move from banana trees and bamboo to a high desert of bare cliffs and irrigated fields.

sections.heading: Why the wind comes every afternoon
paras: Anyone who spends a day in Jomsom learns the rhythm. Mornings are still and clear. Somewhere between nine and eleven o'clock, a breeze starts from the south. By noon it is a strong, steady wind blowing up the valley, carrying dust and grit, and it often keeps going until after sunset before dying away at night.

The cause is the sun. Through the morning, the dry slopes and plateau north of the main range heat up quickly, and the warm air over them rises. Air is drawn in from the south to replace it, and the only low route through the mountains is the Kali Gandaki gorge. Squeezed between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, the flow speeds up, a little like water through a narrow pipe. Meteorologists have studied it for decades as a textbook example of a strong daily valley wind. At night the pattern weakens or reverses, and the valley falls calm again.

sections.heading: What the wind means for your trip
paras: The wind is not dangerous in itself, but it shapes every plan in Mustang. Small planes cannot land safely at Jomsom once it rises, so all flights from Pokhara operate early in the morning, and even a short delay can mean cancellation for the day. Walkers in the valley set off soon after sunrise and try to finish by early afternoon, when walking into the wind becomes tiring and the dust stings.
The wind also makes Mustang feel colder than the thermometer says. A sunny 15 °C afternoon in Kagbeni can feel close to freezing in the open. Plan clothing for wind, not just for temperature.
list: Book the first flight of the day to Jomsom where possible
Keep at least one spare day for flight cancellations
Start walking or driving by 7 or 8 am
Carry a windproof jacket, a buff or scarf, and sunglasses
Use lip balm and moisturiser: the air is very dry
Change camera lenses indoors or in a vehicle

sections.heading: The rain shadow
paras: Pokhara, on the southern side of the Annapurnas, is one of the wettest places in Nepal, with more than 3,000 mm of rain in a typical year, most of it from June to September. Jomsom, less than 80 km to the north-west as the crow flies, gets only a small fraction of that, usually a few hundred millimetres a year at most. Lo Manthang is drier still. Fields survive only where channels bring snowmelt from the mountains, which is why every village in Mustang is a green patch in a brown landscape.

The rain shadow is why Upper Mustang and Dolpo are among the few Nepali treks that work in the monsoon. Skies are often cloudy and there may be light rain, but trails stay mostly dry. The catch is getting there: the road through the wet hills south of Ghasa suffers landslides, and cloud in the gorge cancels flights.

You can watch the rain shadow happen on the drive north from Beni. Around Tatopani the hillsides are thick with forest and the air is humid. By Ghasa pine takes over, by Lete and Kalopani the trees thin, and by Tukuche and Marpha you are among bare slopes and irrigated orchards.

sections.heading: Cold, snow and the winter villages
paras: Winter in Mustang is cold rather than snowy. Jomsom usually sees clear, bright days and frosty nights from December to February, with a few snowfalls a season. Muktinath and the passes above it get more snow, and the Thorong La, the high pass on the Annapurna Circuit to the east, can close for days after a storm. In Upper Mustang, temperatures fall far below freezing at night, water pipes freeze and many households close up and move south to Pokhara or Kathmandu until spring.

That seasonal migration is part of life in Lo. If you visit in late March or early April, you may see families returning with loaded jeeps and horses, reopening houses, cleaning irrigation channels and preparing fields for ploughing.

sections.heading: Planning around the weather by trip type
paras: The same weather affects different journeys in different ways. A pilgrim flying in for two nights at Muktinath worries most about flights and the cold dawn bath. A trekker heading for Lo Manthang cares about afternoon wind on the passes and frosty nights in simple lodges. Someone driving the road from Pokhara is watching for landslides south of Ghasa. When we plan a trip with you, we start with the month and work backwards from these risks.

As a rule of thumb, the shorter and more flight-dependent your trip, the more it matters to travel in the clear months of October, November, April and May. Longer treks and road trips can absorb a delay or two, and they open up the monsoon months, when Mustang is green, quiet and far emptier than the rest of the country.
list: Short flying trips: choose October to May and keep a full spare day
Upper Mustang treks: April to October, including the monsoon months
Road trips from Pokhara: October to May, avoiding the landslide season
Winter visits: Lower Mustang only, with warm clothing and flexible plans
Photography: late September to November for the clearest air

sections.heading: Birds and the autumn wind
paras: The Kali Gandaki is not only a route for people. In autumn, flocks of demoiselle cranes migrating south from Central Asia toward India use the valley as a passage through the Himalaya, and on clear October days you may see long V-shaped skeins high over Jomsom or Kalopani. Birds of prey also follow the valley. Local people have watched the cranes for generations, and their calls carry far in the still morning air before the wind starts.

Whatever month you come, let the valley set the timetable. Be up early, be out in the calm, and when the wind arrives, find a warm lodge kitchen, order a pot of tea and watch the prayer flags stream north.

faqs.q: Why is it so windy in Jomsom?
faqs.a: As the sun heats the dry land north of the Himalaya each morning, warm air rises and air is drawn in from the south. The easiest route for it is the Kali Gandaki gorge between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna, which squeezes and speeds up the flow. The result is a strong wind from late morning until evening on most days of the year.

faqs.q: Why do Jomsom flights only fly in the morning?
faqs.a: Because the afternoon wind makes landing small planes at Jomsom unsafe. Flights from Pokhara operate from early morning until the wind rises, usually by late morning. If cloud or early wind delays the first flights, the day's remaining flights are often cancelled. Always allow a spare day in your plans when flying to or from Jomsom.

faqs.q: Does it rain in Mustang during the monsoon?
faqs.a: Very little compared with the rest of Nepal. Mustang lies in the rain shadow of the Annapurna and Dhaulagiri ranges, so from June to September Jomsom and Upper Mustang see cloudy days and light rain, but trails stay mostly dry. The problem is access: landslides on the road south of Ghasa and cloud that cancels flights.

faqs.q: What is the best month to visit Mustang?
faqs.a: October is the best single month, with clear skies and settled weather, followed by April and May, when Tiji takes place in Lo Manthang. September and November are also good. Upper Mustang works in the monsoon months too. December to February is cold, and many Upper Mustang lodges close.

faqs.q: How cold does it get in Mustang?
faqs.a: In Jomsom, winter days are often around 5 to 10 °C in the sun with nights well below freezing, and the wind makes it feel colder. Upper Mustang is several degrees colder at every season. Even in May and October, nights in Lo Manthang can drop below freezing. Bring a warm jacket and a sleeping bag for teahouse stays.

Yes, especially in the afternoons and along the roads. The wind lifts fine dust from the riverbeds and tracks, and jeeps add more. A buff or scarf over the nose and mouth helps, as do sunglasses. Photographers should protect their gear and avoid changing lenses outdoors in the wind.

Occasionally. Jomsom gets a few snowfalls in most winters, usually between December and February, but snow rarely lasts long on the valley floor. Muktinath and the higher villages get more snow, and passes like the Thorong La can close after storms. Clear, cold and windy days are more typical than heavy snow.

faqs.q: When is the wind calmest in the Kali Gandaki?
faqs.a: Early morning, from dawn until about nine or ten o'clock, is usually calm, which is why walkers and flights start early. The wind tends to fade again after sunset. Calm days happen, especially in cloudy or stormy weather, but for planning, assume a strong wind from late morning to early evening.

faqs.q: When do demoiselle cranes fly over Mustang?
faqs.a: Demoiselle cranes migrate south through the Kali Gandaki valley in autumn, mostly in late September and October, on their way from Central Asia toward India. On clear mornings you may see or hear large flocks flying high over Jomsom, Marpha and Kalopani. Return migration in spring is less visible.
